Circuit examples and the comparison with classical sampling are planned. Numerical query or runtime claims will be added with their assumptions and evidence.

Amplitude estimation extends the search components into a scalar estimation task. The chapter will connect preparation, amplification, measurement, and confidence requirements using the survey’s application perspective 

Dalzell et al., 2025.

The task is to estimate a with a specified error and confidence level. The preparation circuit and its inverse are part of the implementation contract.

The ledger will count preparation and inverse-preparation calls, reflections, controlled operations where used, shot counts, and classical estimation. It will distinguish query complexity from compiled gate cost and physical execution time. Confidence requirements will be shared across the quantum and classical comparison.

The estimator will be tested against exact probabilities for several small instances. Coverage checks will assess the reported intervals over repeated experiments. Resource estimates will include the implemented preparation circuit rather than treating it as a unit-cost oracle.

Algorithmic estimation error, coherent synthesis approximation, sampling confidence, and physical faults will be kept separate. Synthesis approximations change the probability being estimated and require a bias allowance. The current bounded-observable helper covers a fixed scalar mean under declared assumptions; it does not automatically establish confidence for an adaptive amplitude-estimation protocol.

Publish decomposed logical counts and a conditional physical frontier for the complete schedule. Compare classical sampling of the same preparation task at the same output tolerance and confidence. Include preprocessing and classical postprocessing before drawing an application-level conclusion.

Compare estimated values with exact probabilities for interior values and boundary cases near zero and one. Separate a deterministic ideal-distribution check from finite-shot statistical validation. Grover search amplifies the probability of a marked item using a reversible predicate and a reflection about a uniform superposition 

Grover, 1996. It is a useful first implementation because its circuit is small enough to inspect and its ideal success probability has a closed form. The survey gives the broader application and end-to-end complexity context 

Dalzell et al., 2025.

Note

Implementation status

The three-qubit demo is simulated and checked against the mathematical prediction during the site build. The generator supports other sizes. The exported circuit includes the oracle and diffuser decomposed into gates; its arbitrary rotations still require synthesis before fault-tolerant costing. The separate 

surface-code baseline records the physical assumptions and estimator output.

There are N=2^n computational basis states and exactly one marked state m. The phase oracle applies -1 to \lvert m\rangle and leaves every other basis state unchanged. Our explicit oracle compares the register to a known integer using X gates and a multi-controlled phase flip. This is a teaching example: knowing the target already solves the classical problem. A practical search application must replace it with a reversible problem predicate and count that predicate’s construction, evaluation, and uncomputation.

The notebook uses Qiskit core, an open-source circuit library released under Apache 2.0. The circuit generator is an original implementation using Qiskit core. See the 

upstream repository and the 

downloadable implementation source.

We prepare three qubits in the uniform superposition, mark integer 5 (bitstring 101), and apply two Grover iterations. Qiskit displays bitstrings with the most significant bit first; circuit wire q[0] represents the least significant bit.

The circuit below is reused directly from the saved output of the executable notebook.

n_qubits, marked = 3, 5
iterations = optimal_iterations(n_qubits)
circuit = build_grover_circuit(n_qubits, marked, iterations)
circuit.draw(output='mpl', fold=32)



Let \theta=\arcsin(1/\sqrt{N}). After r iterations, the ideal probability of the marked state isP(m)=\sin^2((2r+1)\theta).

For N=8 and r=2, this is 0.9453125. The exact statevector simulation checks this value. Sampling a real device would additionally introduce shot noise and device errors.

First- and second-order product formulas implement dynamics with state, operator and observable checks. Taylor LCU has actual PREPARE/SELECT, uncomputation and a measured/reset postselection schedule. Qubitization access and a degree-14 QSP cosine filter are checked. Full complex QSP evolution and amplitude amplification remain planned. Physical estimates await a reviewed rotation-synthesis adapter. No hardware advantage or formal proof is claimed.

Use three spins on an open chain withH=A+B,\quad A=Z_0Z_1+Z_1Z_2,\quad B=0.7(X_0+X_1+X_2).

The coupling J=1 defines the energy unit, \hbar=1, and time is t=1 in inverse coupling units. Prepare |\psi_0\rangle=|000\rangle. The state task approximates U(t)|\psi_0\rangle for U(t)=e^{-iHt}; the observable task estimates \langle Z_0\rangle after evolution. These outputs have different repetition costs. The exact small classical observable is approximately 0.404255857287.

The input is an explicit Pauli coefficient list. Qiskit labels read q[2] q[1] q[0]: the terms are IZZ, ZZI, IIX, IXI, XII. The observable assigns +1 to bit 0 equal to zero and -1 to bit 0 equal to one. The zero basis input needs no preparation gates; a device still needs initialization. No external data loading is modeled.

For an approximation V, report spectral operator error \|V-U\|_2, state-vector error \|V\psi_0-U\psi_0\|_2, state infidelity and observable bias separately. Vector error retains phase; infidelity does not. For normalized states, a state-vector error \epsilon bounds this observable bias by 2\epsilon.

Let \delta=t/r. Applying an A layer followed chronologically by a B layer givesV_1(t;r)=\left(e^{-iB\delta}e^{-iA\delta}\right)^r.

Applying half an A layer, a full B layer and half an A layer givesV_2(t;r)=\left(e^{-iA\delta/2}e^{-iB\delta}e^{-iA\delta/2}\right)^r.

These are Lie–Trotter and symmetric Strang splittings 

Trotter, 1959

Strang, 1968. Modern commutator bounds explain their approximation error 

Childs et al., 2021; the curves here are numerical results for this instance.

Terms within each layer commute. Each e^{-ic\delta Z_iZ_{i+1}} uses CX–R_Z(2c\delta)–CX; each e^{-ic\delta X_i} uses R_X(2c\delta). Half layers halve the angle. The generator uses these primitive operations directly and never appends a dense evolution gate.

At 32 symmetric steps, operator error is approximately 5.0261\times10^{-4}, state-vector error 4.0545\times10^{-4} and observable bias 1.5912\times10^{-4}. Doubling steps in the tested range approximately halves the first-order operator error and quarters the second-order operator error.

The two formulas give equal Z_0 expectations on this input although their states and operators differ. Here V_2=e^{-iA\delta/2}V_1e^{+iA\delta/2}; the initial state is an eigenstate of A and Z_0 commutes with A. Boundary phases are invisible to this observable. An observable-only check would miss the first-order circuit’s larger evolution error.

For a segment \delta=t/r, formT_K(\delta)=\sum_{k=0}^K\frac{(-i\delta H)^k}{k!}=\sum_j b_j P_j,\qquad s=\sum_j|b_j|.

Bounded classical preprocessing multiplies Pauli strings, combines identical strings and removes only exact floating-point zeros. Its actual normalization differs from the unaggregated word-series normalization. This preprocessing can grow exponentially; it is not the scalable word-indexed access model of the truncated-Taylor algorithm 

Berry et al., 2015.

A binary tree of controlled R_Y rotations implements\mathrm{PREPARE}|0\rangle=\sum_j\sqrt{|b_j|/s}|j\rangle.

Indexed X/Y/Z gates and coefficient phases implement \mathrm{SELECT}=\sum_j|j\rangle\langle j|\otimes e^{i\arg b_j}P_j. Padded labels apply identity. PREPARE, SELECT and inverse PREPARE give a unitary whose zero-label block is T_K/s. Tests compare that actual block with an independent polynomial matrix, including negative/complex coefficients and bit ordering.

For K=4 and segment counts r=1,2,4,8, we check the unnormalized polynomial operator against U, the conditional state before final system readout against U|000\rangle and the observable against its exact value. Conditional-state error and acceptance probability are separate.

lcu_rows = []
for segments in (1, 2, 4, 8):
    access = lcu.build_taylor_lcu(terms, 1 / segments, 4)
    conditional, success, per_segment = lcu.postselected_lcu_evolution(access, initial, segments)
    value = float(np.vdot(conditional, Z0 @ conditional).real)
    lcu_rows.append({"segments": segments, "terms": len(access.terms), "normalization": access.normalization,
                     "conditional_state_error": float(np.linalg.norm(conditional - exact @ initial)),
                     "observable_error": abs(value - exact_z), "whole_attempt_success": success,
                     "attempts_for_one_measured_trial_99_percent": lcu.postselection_attempts(success, .01)})
display(pd.DataFrame(lcu_rows))



Every segment must return zero label bits. Ancillas are reset for reuse; an attempt runs all segments and finally measures every system wire in Z. The exported attempt circuits include initial resets, all access/uncomputation, label measurement/reset and final readout; their output is an accepted measured trial. The conditional state checked above describes the system immediately before that final readout. Whole-attempt acceptance is the product of state-dependent conditional probabilities. At eight segments, ideal acceptance is about 0.001015, requiring thousands of complete attempts for one accepted measured trial with 99% confidence. The ledger also records a capped retry budget for many accepted observable shots, charging the complete schedule each time.

Oblivious amplitude amplification remains planned. It is not supplied by the postselection circuit. State/observable values come from ideal simulation; approximation errors exclude rotation synthesis, physical faults and finite-shot noise. This unamplified demonstration is not an efficiency comparison with product formulas.

The five Hamiltonian terms have \alpha=\sum_j|c_j|=4.1. Explicit PREPARE and signed Pauli SELECT give the Hermitian involutionB=\mathrm{PREPARE}^\dagger\mathrm{SELECT}\,\mathrm{PREPARE},\qquad\langle0|B|0\rangle=H/\alpha.

Tests check the actual block. A reflection about the zero-label subspace creates the qubitization walk and its invariant-subspace identity is checked 

Low & Chuang, 2019.

The QSP module documents its scalar matrix convention and phase ordering. Fourteen calls to B and fifteen frozen phases produce a degree-14 real polynomial approximating \cos(4.1x)/2 on [-1,1]. A flag coherently combines the +\phi and -\phi branches to extract the real part, sharing block calls. The phase JSON records a deterministic SciPy fit, independent dense-grid residual, Chebyshev-coefficient discrepancy and analytic polynomial-tail bound. Tests compare the actual circuit block to \cos(H)/2, separately from the scalar phase check 

Low & Chuang, 2017

Gilyén et al., 2019.

The circuit-block error is approximately 3.40\times10^{-9} and ideal acceptance on |000\rangle is 0.1782034. These are filter results. Full complex QSP dynamics remains planned: this filter has conditional normalization and does not implement e^{-iH}. A single parity-constrained real polynomial does not supply both even cosine and odd sine. A later circuit must coherently combine them and count success/amplification. The current phase fit does not certify arbitrary rotation synthesis.

A product-formula observable-accuracy proposal of 0.05 allocates 0.01 bias to Hamiltonian approximation, 0.01 to coherent synthesis and 0.03 to sampling. The checked r=32 operator error meets its allowance of 0.005; synthesis is pending. For independent \pm1 samples, Hoeffding givesN\geq\left\lceil\frac{2\log(2/\eta_{\rm stat})}{\epsilon_{\rm stat}^2}\right\rceil=13315,
\quad\epsilon_{\rm stat}=0.03,\quad\eta_{\rm stat}=0.005.

Separately, a proposed total physical-failure probability of 0.005 gives a per-shot allowance 0.005/N by a union bound. Coherent norm error is not stochastic failure. A conservative synthesis proposal divides its 0.005 operator allowance across counted arbitrary rotations via a telescoping sum of gate errors. A reviewed synthesis adapter is required before surface-code estimates.

Preparing this normalized state differs from returning all classical entries of x. The report will select a state metric or a named observable and include its measurement procedure. If the requested answer needs a norm, an entire vector, or several observables, that additional readout must be specified and charged.

records.content:
Number the vertices 0,1,2,3 and supply the edge list\mathcal E=\{(0,1),(1,2),(2,3),(0,3)\}.

For an assignment z=(z_0,z_1,z_2,z_3), the cut size and cost operator areC(z)=\sum_{(u,v)\in\mathcal E}[z_u\ne z_v],\qquad
C=\sum_{(u,v)\in\mathcal E}\frac{I-Z_uZ_v}{2}.

The classical maximum is four, attained by the two alternating assignments. Qiskit wire q[0] is the least significant bit, so displayed strings read z_3z_2z_1z_0; the optimal strings are 0101 and 1010. Enumeration evaluates the edge predicate directly rather than consulting the quantum objective routine.

Starting from |+\rangle^{\otimes4}, one QAOA layer applies|\psi(\gamma,\beta)\rangle=
e^{-i\beta\sum_j X_j}e^{-i\gamma C}|+\rangle^{\otimes4}.

The optimizer minimizes f(\gamma,\beta)=-\langle C\rangle. Angles are radians. Our gate convention is R_P(\alpha)=e^{-i\alpha P/2}: the mixer uses rx(2*beta) on every vertex. For each edge, the phase circuit is cx(u,v); rz(-gamma,v); cx(u,v). This realizes e^{+i\gamma Z_uZ_v/2}; the omitted identity contribution changes only the global phase. There is no dense-matrix oracle or unexplained access operation.



For this cycle and one layer, an independent expression for the expected cut is\langle C\rangle=2+\sin(4\beta)\sin(2\gamma).

Thus \gamma=\pi/4, \beta=\pi/8 gives mean cut three, compared with the classical maximum four. The ratio 3/4 describes an expected cut on this instance. It does not mean every draw has cut three. At these analytic angles, the probabilities of cut sizes zero, two, and four are 1/32, 14/32, and 17/32. Each maximum-cut bitstring has probability 17/64. The saved plot and run record report the corresponding numerical distribution for the fitted angles.





All edges are diagonal in the computational basis. One all-Z measurement produces an assignment and evaluates all four edge contributions together. For a fixed optimized state with best-cut probability p_\star, N independent ideal draws contain a maximum cut with probability 1-(1-p_\star)^N. At the analytic angles, seven draws give success above 0.99. This calculation assumes ideal preparations at those fixed angles and independent draws; it does not predict optimizer success or noisy-device performance.

Use dimensionless coefficients and the HamiltonianH=-Z_0-Z_1+\frac12 X_0X_1.

In basis order |q_1q_0\rangle=|00\rangle,|01\rangle,|10\rangle,|11\rangle, its matrix isH=\begin{pmatrix}
-2&0&0&1/2\\
0&0&1/2&0\\
0&1/2&0&0\\
1/2&0&0&2
\end{pmatrix}.

Its eigenvalues are -\sqrt{17}/2,-1/2,1/2,\sqrt{17}/2, so the reference ground energy is E_0=-\sqrt{17}/2\approx-2.061552813. This is a stated teaching Hamiltonian, rather than a molecule or chemistry workload with uncounted integral preparation.

Prepare |00\rangle, apply ry(theta,0), and then cx(0,1). The resulting state is|\psi(\theta)\rangle=
\cos(\theta/2)|00\rangle+\sin(\theta/2)|11\rangle.



The independent scalar expectation isE(\theta)=-2\cos\theta+\frac12\sin\theta.

Its minimum is the full matrix ground energy, attained at \theta=-\arctan(1/4) modulo 2\pi. This ansatz can represent the exact ground state of this particular Hamiltonian. The generator and notebook compare the circuit expectation, matrix eigenvalue, and scalar formula; this expressibility statement does not extend to a general Hamiltonian or ansatz.



Finite-shot energy evaluation uses two groups. In the all-Z group, one bitstring yields the joint value -Z_0-Z_1; its sample variance includes covariance of the Z terms. In the all-X group, apply H to both qubits before computational-basis measurement and score \tfrac12X_0X_1. Adding the group means estimates total energy. The measurement protocol requires a fresh ansatz preparation for each shot, and H basis changes and final measurements appear in the exports. The implementation obtains each group’s statevector probabilities and draws its counts classically. Shot noise can put a sampled energy below E_0 even though the exact expectation obeys the variational bound.

The original optimizer is a small coordinate polling routine. It evaluates the initial point, then every negative and positive coordinate displacement in a fixed order. If the best candidate reduces the minimized objective by more than 

10-12, it accepts that candidate; otherwise it halves the step. The initial step is 0.4 radians. It stops when the step falls below 

10-6 radians or after 128 sweeps, and records which condition stopped each run. Coordinates are wrapped modulo 2\pi.

QAOA initial points are (\gamma,\beta)=(0.2,0.1),(0.6,0.4),(-0.3,0.25). VQE initial angles are 0.6,-1.1,2.2. Every optimization objective uses an exact ideal statevector, with zero measurement shots. The run record retains accepted points, rejected candidates, iterations, evaluation counts, parameters, elapsed objective time, and total classical optimization time. Wall-clock timings include the classical simulator and are machine-dependent; they are not hardware execution times.



The primary fitted angles are then evaluated in separate ideal finite-shot experiments with seeds 7, 19, and 41, using 2,048 shots per measurement group per seed. Samples are drawn classically from statevector probabilities; repeated physical circuits are not executed. These experiments do not feed sampled objectives back to the optimizer. They report counts, sampled objectives, exact expectations, sample standard errors, and achieved output quality. Changing initialization probes optimization variability; changing the sampling seed probes readout variability. Neither experiment tests device noise, error mitigation, nor convergence of a sampled optimizer.

Given an integer N and a base a coprime to N, order finding seeks the smallest positive r such thata^r \equiv 1 \pmod N.

Factoring combines sampled information about the order with classical number-theoretic processing. A complete run must include unsuccessful base choices and sampling outcomes in its success accounting.

The resource ledger will count modular arithmetic, control registers, ancillas, uncomputation, phase precision, and repetitions. It will report classical preprocessing and factor reconstruction separately. Small demonstration instances will be labeled with any simplifications that prevent their direct use as scaling estimates.

Classical modular exponentiation will check small reversible arithmetic blocks over their valid input domain. The run will verify the recovered order and factors. Register layout and ancilla cleanup will be tested before physical-resource estimates are published.

Record the integer N, its bit width, the permitted base-selection procedure, the required probability of obtaining a nontrivial factor, and the arithmetic design. Order finding for one fixed base is a subroutine; its cost alone does not cover unsuccessful base choices, unsuccessful phase samples, or factor reconstruction.

An arithmetic box named “modular exponentiation” is not a primitive-gate resource count. The generator must expose its reversible implementation. Report both bit-width scaling and concrete decomposed small instances; a circuit simplified using a known order or factor needs a separate pedagogical label.

Allocate phase-estimation precision, inverse-QFT approximation, and coherent rotation synthesis before mapping the circuit to error correction. Keep approximation allowances separate from the probabilities of sampling failure and physical faults. The current shared estimator supports bound static circuits with final measurements; adaptive phase estimation needs a branch-aware extension.

Use the 

fault-tolerance appendix to specify the code, decoder, physical errors, operation times, factory choices, and scheduling model. The frozen 

Grover surface-code report illustrates the reporting format; its numerical result is not a bound for factoring.

Arbitrary-angle costs from the shared synthesis helper are conditional mean-fit projections. They do not supply a concrete synthesized circuit, an instance approximation certificate, or a worst-case runtime guarantee. A future comparison must hold the factoring task and its accuracy/success requirements fixed while changing the implementation. No quantum-advantage claim follows from the planned resource ledger.

Verification protocol

These checks are planned acceptance criteria. This page contains no executed Shor result or reproduced formal proof. Method-specific evidence will link to the implemented circuit, pinned environment, and report.

For small registers, compare each modular multiplication with classical integer arithmetic on every valid basis input. Define the circuit’s behavior on basis states outside 0\leq x<N as well: a reversible circuit must have a consistent unitary extension over the entire register. Test the control-off identity, the control-on permutation, register ordering, and restoration of every clean ancilla.

Compare the explicit circuit with its decomposed export up to global phase. A simulator’s classical arithmetic callback or a dense matrix representing the desired permutation is a reference oracle, not evidence that the scalable arithmetic generator has been implemented.

Choose tiny instances with a classically known multiplicative order. Record the phase samples, the continued-fraction procedure, and every candidate order rejected or accepted. Verify a^r\bmod N=1 and, when the claimed result is the order, exclude smaller candidates. Validate that returned factors are nontrivial and divide N exactly.

The success test must include failed samples and base choices. Do not select a favorable sample after seeing the answer or compile the answer into the demonstration circuit. Fix a stopping/retry procedure before collecting evidence, then check its declared failure calculation.

Shor’s paper is the algorithm reference. Small exhaustive arithmetic checks cover those tested register sizes; they do not prove correctness for every integer or certify a surface-code realization. A future formal artifact must identify its arithmetic semantics, theorem, toolchain, and connection to the generator.

For a finite Hamiltonian and a specified inverse temperature \beta in inverse energy units, the target state is\rho_\beta=\frac{e^{-\beta H}}{Z_\beta},\qquad Z_\beta=\operatorname{Tr}(e^{-\beta H}).

The implementation will distinguish preparing this density operator, preparing a purification, and estimating a chosen thermal observable. It must specify the representation of H, its energy reference, the input state, approximation metric, confidence and failure allowance. The preparation method and its normalization, initial overlap and any spectral assumptions remain to be chosen.

The ledger will include actual Hamiltonian access, filtering or channel construction, purification ancillas, postselection/amplification if used, discarded systems, measurement, repetitions and classical preprocessing. A tiny normalized matrix exponential will check the selected circuit once it exists. Low-temperature preparation and high-temperature observable estimation will not be treated as the same workload.

An open-system instance will specify an initial density operator \rho(0) and either a finite channel or a time-independent Markovian GKSL generator 

Lindblad, 1976

Gorini et al., 1976:\mathcal L(\rho)=-i[H,\rho]+\sum_k\left(L_k\rho L_k^\dagger-
\tfrac12\{L_k^\dagger L_k,\rho\}\right),\qquad \rho(t)=e^{t\mathcal L}\rho(0).

The next implementation must define the Hamiltonian, jump operators, rates, units and time; choose a requested state or observable; and state a trace-distance or channel-error requirement and sampling confidence. If rates are given separately, L_k=\sqrt{\gamma_k}A_k. General open-system evolution need not have this semigroup form. A density-matrix exponential alone will not implement this quantum task.

Circuit evidence will include an actual channel or dilation, environment ancillas, preparation and uncomputation where applicable, reset/discard operations, and the measurement schedule. Comparisons will preserve the same generator, input, time, observable and error metric. Approximation error, statistical error and physical faults will have separate budgets. The first bounded example and its method remain to be selected and implemented.

Return to quantum simulation.

An ideal circuit specifies logical operations. A physical processor must implement them while qubits, gates, measurements, and idle periods can fail. Fault tolerance encodes information across many physical qubits and repeatedly measures error syndromes. These measurements reveal information about errors while preserving the encoded quantum information. The result is a logical operation with a modeled failure probability and a physical space and time cost.

The surface code uses local stabilizer checks on a two-dimensional layout. Its code distance characterizes the smallest undetectable logical error. Increasing distance consumes more physical qubits and more syndrome rounds; the required distance depends on the noise model, decoder, and permitted failure probability. A threshold is a property of those assumptions, rather than a guarantee supplied by the algorithm’s logical qubit count. 

Fowler and colleagues’ surface-code review introduces these constructions and their implementation costs.

Layout matters. Logical data patches, routing space, temporary ancillas, and measurement procedures contribute to the footprint. Operations performed through lattice surgery occupy patches for several syndrome rounds. A logical circuit’s abstract gate depth therefore needs a timing and scheduling model before it becomes elapsed physical time.

Clifford operations preserve stabilizer structure. Universal computation also needs non-Clifford operations, commonly T gates or equivalent injected resources. A factory distills noisy resource states into states suitable for logical computation. Its footprint, throughput, output error, and number of parallel copies must be included in the report. Factories can dominate a small demonstration.

Arbitrary-angle rotations introduce another approximation step: select a synthesis method and allocate precision, then account for the resulting gates or resource states. Counting an undecomposed multi-controlled operation as one physical gate hides substantial work. Likewise, a synthesis cost formula alone does not supply the actual gate sequence or certify its approximation error.

A useful ledger records four different quantities: algorithmic approximation, coherent synthesis approximation, measurement precision and confidence, and physical faults. For one scalar observable, independently justified bias bounds and a statistical interval can be allocated within an absolute error target. A physical fault allowance remains a probability; it is not interchangeable with an observable’s absolute error.

For repeated executions, state whether trials are serial or parallel and allocate failure probability across the complete run. For a hybrid optimizer, include every parameter setting, measurement group, and stopping rule. Confidence for one fixed scalar mean does not establish optimizer convergence or simultaneous confidence for an entire energy sum.

The 

frozen Grover report is a concrete illustration with explicit circuit and hardware assumptions. Other algorithms must supply their own preparation, access, approximation, and output costs. Their reports cannot inherit Grover’s physical counts.

The general resource helper uses a pinned QDK synthesis model based on a mean fit. Reports involving arbitrary rotations are conditional resource projections: no concrete synthesis sequence or instance-level approximation certificate is produced. Physical reliability also depends on the declared surface-code and factory models. See the 

QDK model documentation and 

reported quantities.

Compare designs at the same problem instance, output, precision, confidence, and physical assumptions. Publish peak physical qubits and elapsed time as a Pareto frontier. Peak qubits multiplied by runtime is a useful named summary; a detailed occupation schedule provides the integral of occupied qubits over time. Neither metric alone establishes an application advantage.

Qiskit: Fault Tolerant Quantum Computation, Lesson 16 provides a video introduction to the mechanisms behind this appendix. The lesson opens only when selected; it is supplementary to the recorded assumptions in each resource report.

The mathematical task is to connect a problem specification to a circuit and a checkable output. This primer collects notation used by the algorithm chapters. It complements the 

quantum-physics primer; no background in formal proof software is required.

A ket |v\rangle is a complex column vector; its bra \langle v| is the conjugate transpose. The inner product and Euclidean norm are\langle v|w\rangle=\sum_j\overline{v_j}w_j,
\qquad \|v\|_2=\sqrt{\langle v|v\rangle}.

Orthogonal vectors have zero inner product. An orthonormal basis gives coordinates without changing lengths. Normalized state vectors have unit norm, while input data vectors may require a separate normalization factor. 

IBM’s inner-products lesson develops these conventions.

Two registers combine by a tensor product: |v\rangle\otimes|w\rangle. Dimensions multiply, so n qubits have 2^n basis states. A joint vector need not factor into individual-register vectors; this is the mathematical possibility behind entanglement. Register order and bit order must match the generator, simulator, and classical comparison. A statevector containing every amplitude therefore has very different storage requirements from a circuit description.

Matrices act linearly on vectors. The adjoint A^\dagger conjugates and transposes; a unitary satisfies U^\dagger U=I and preserves inner products. A Hermitian matrix satisfies H^\dagger=H and has real eigenvalues with an orthonormal eigenbasis:H|u_j\rangle=\lambda_j|u_j\rangle,\qquad
H=\sum_j\lambda_j|u_j\rangle\langle u_j|.

Phase estimation targets the phase in U|u_j\rangle=e^{2\pi i\phi_j}|u_j\rangle. The prepared state’s overlap with the relevant eigenvector affects the chance of obtaining that phase.

Watch Gilbert Strang’s 

MIT 18.06 video, “Lecture 21: Eigenvalues and eigenvectors” for the underlying eigenvector equation. The official lesson includes a video and transcript; quantum phase estimation applies this idea to unitary operators.

A norm makes “close” quantitative. The operator norm\|A\|=\sup_{\|v\|_2=1}\|Av\|_2

measures the largest amplification of a vector. The trace norm \|A\|_1 is the sum of singular values, and the Frobenius norm \|A\|_F=\sqrt{\operatorname{Tr}(A^\dagger A)} measures all entries together. These norms give different error guarantees.

For Hermitian H, define f(H) by applying f to its eigenvalues. If a polynomial p approximates f uniformly on an interval containing the spectrum, then\sup_{x\in[a,b]}|p(x)-f(x)|\leq\epsilon
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\|p(H)-f(H)\|\leq\epsilon.

This motivates polynomial methods for evolution and inversion. QSP/QSVT circuits also impose encoding, boundedness, and parity conditions; an arbitrary polynomial fit alone is insufficient. 

PennyLane’s QSVT introduction explains this connection.

Linear-system algorithms must additionally track conditioning. For an invertible matrix, the spectral condition number is \kappa=\sigma_{\max}/\sigma_{\min}. Small singular values can make inversion sensitive and expensive. Producing a state proportional to A^{-1}b also leaves its normalization and requested readout to be accounted for. It does not directly return a classical list of every solution component.

For independent preparations with success probability p, R trials all fail with probability (1-p)^R. Repetition costs belong in the algorithm estimate.

For independent Bernoulli outcomes X_1,\ldots,X_M with common mean p, the frequency \hat p=M^{-1}\sum_iX_i estimates that probability. Hoeffding’s bound gives\Pr(|\hat p-p|\geq\epsilon)\leq2e^{-2M\epsilon^2}.

Thus M\geq\ln(2/\delta)/(2\epsilon^2) suffices for confidence at least 1-\delta. 

John Duchi’s Stanford notes state the independence and boundedness assumptions. Sampling confidence controls random variation; it does not remove a biased circuit or an inaccurate model. Specify those errors separately when comparing quantum and classical outputs.

Quantum algorithms use quantum physics to transform information and extract a specified result. This appendix introduces the finite-dimensional language used throughout the handbook. Read it alongside the 

mathematics primer, then follow the quantities you actually need to reproduce an algorithm.

A pure state is a normalized complex vector |\psi\rangle. For one qubit,|\psi\rangle=\alpha|0\rangle+\beta|1\rangle,
\qquad |\alpha|^2+|\beta|^2=1.

Relative phases affect interference. Multiplying the whole vector by the same phase leaves its physical state unchanged. A state describes the system; an observable describes a measurable quantity. Observables are Hermitian operators, such as the Pauli Z operator or the Hamiltonian H, which represents energy.

A density matrix also describes mixtures and subsystems entangled with an environment:\rho=\sum_j p_j|\psi_j\rangle\langle\psi_j|,
\qquad p_j\geq0,\quad \sum_jp_j=1.

It is positive semidefinite and has trace one. Pure states have \rho=|\psi\rangle\langle\psi|; different ensembles can describe the same mixed state. Ignoring part of a joint system gives its reduced density matrix by a partial trace. 

IBM’s density-matrix lesson develops this broader description.

For example, |+\rangle=(|0\rangle+|1\rangle)/\sqrt2 and the mixture \rho=I/2 both give equal computational-basis probabilities. They differ when measured in the X basis: the pure state always gives the +1 outcome, whereas the mixture gives either outcome equally often. Matching one measurement distribution therefore does not establish that two states agree.

For an observable A=\sum_a aP_a, a projective measurement returns eigenvalue a with Born-rule probabilityp(a)=\operatorname{Tr}(P_a\rho),
\qquad \langle A\rangle=\operatorname{Tr}(A\rho).

The projectors P_a include any degeneracy. Measuring a pure state in the computational basis gives p(x)=|\langle x|\psi\rangle|^2. One shot produces an outcome; estimating an expectation generally requires repeated preparations and measurements.

For the physical connection between eigenvectors and measurement, watch Barton Zwiebach’s 

MIT 8.04 video, “Completeness of eigenvectors and measurement postulate”. Its official lesson page includes the video and transcript.

Closed-system evolution is unitary:\rho(t)=U(t)\rho(0)U(t)^\dagger,\qquad
U(t)=e^{-iHt/\hbar}

for a time-independent Hamiltonian. Circuit gates approximate or compose such transformations; the simulation chapters usually set \hbar=1.

Noise, discarded ancillas, and measurements averaged over their outcomes require quantum channels. A completely positive, trace-preserving map has a Kraus representation\mathcal E(\rho)=\sum_jK_j\rho K_j^\dagger,
\qquad \sum_jK_j^\dagger K_j=I.

Complete positivity ensures valid states even when the input is entangled with another system. Trace preservation retains total probability. A selected measurement branch can instead decrease the trace; that trace records the branch’s success probability. 

IBM’s channel representations explain the channel viewpoint and its implementations.

For a finite-dimensional Hamiltonian, the Gibbs state at inverse temperature \beta=1/(k_BT) is\rho_\beta=\frac{e^{-\beta H}}{Z(\beta)},
\qquad Z(\beta)=\operatorname{Tr}(e^{-\beta H}).

The partition function normalizes the state; exponentiating a Hamiltonian alone does not produce a normalized density matrix. Energy eigenstates receive weights proportional to e^{-\beta E_j}. See David Tong’s 

statistical-physics notes on the canonical ensemble.

Choose an output metric before estimating resources. A search task needs a correct answer with stated probability. An energy task needs observable accuracy and sampling confidence. A state-preparation task may use trace distance D(\rho,\sigma)=\tfrac12\|\rho-\sigma\|_1, which bounds changes in measurement-event probabilities. Fidelity measures similarity; specify whether it is squared or unsquared, as 

IBM’s fidelity lesson emphasizes. The

Run the following cells in Binder or a local JupyterLab kernel to use Python controls. The published book shows saved circuit and probability outputs; its separate browser explorer computes the ideal probability formula.

The notebook controls regenerate the actual Qiskit circuit and exact statevector for 2–6 qubits and 0–12 Grover iterations. The marked value adapts to the register size. Every evaluation checks the simulated marked-state probability against the analytic formula.

import os
import numpy as np


def simulate_interactive_case(n_qubits, marked, iterations):
    """Bounded ideal simulation shared by the controls and deterministic checks."""
    if not 2 <= n_qubits <= 6:
        raise ValueError("Live controls support 2–6 qubits")
    if not 0 <= iterations <= 12:
        raise ValueError("Live controls support 0–12 iterations")
    marked = min(max(int(marked), 0), 2**n_qubits - 1)
    circuit = build_grover_circuit(n_qubits, marked, iterations)
    probabilities = Statevector.from_instruction(circuit).probabilities()
    expected = expected_success_probability(n_qubits, iterations)
    np.testing.assert_allclose(probabilities[marked], expected, atol=1e-10, rtol=0)
    return circuit, probabilities, marked, expected


for validation_n in range(2, 7):
    for validation_marked in (0, 2**validation_n - 1):
        for validation_iterations in (0, optimal_iterations(validation_n), 12):
            simulate_interactive_case(validation_n, validation_marked, validation_iterations)
print("Validated 30 bounded cases; every live evaluation also checks the analytic probability.")




# The book build skips widget creation so it never publishes inert controls.
# Binder and local kernels display live controls when this cell is run.
if os.environ.get("OPENQUANTUM_STATIC_BUILD") == "1":
    print("Live Python controls are available when this notebook is run in Binder or JupyterLab.")
else:
    import ipywidgets as widgets
    from IPython.display import display

    n_control = widgets.IntSlider(value=3, min=2, max=6, description="Qubits", continuous_update=False)
    marked_control = widgets.IntSlider(value=5, min=0, max=7, description="Marked", continuous_update=False)
    iterations_control = widgets.IntSlider(value=2, min=0, max=12, description="Iterations", continuous_update=False)

    def update_marked_range(change):
        marked_control.max = 2**change["new"] - 1
        marked_control.value = min(marked_control.value, marked_control.max)

    n_control.observe(update_marked_range, names="value")

    def render_live_case(n_qubits, marked, iterations):
        circuit, probabilities, marked, expected = simulate_interactive_case(n_qubits, marked, iterations)
        target = f"{marked:0{n_qubits}b}"
        print(f"Target {target}; {iterations} iterations; first-peak choice {optimal_iterations(n_qubits)}")
        print(f"Statevector probability {probabilities[marked]:.10f}; analytic probability {expected:.10f}")
        print("Ideal circuit: no device noise or fault-tolerant resource model is applied here.")
        circuit_figure = circuit.draw(output="mpl", fold=32, scale=0.65)
        display(circuit_figure)
        plt.close(circuit_figure)
        figure, axis = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 3.2))
        indices = list(range(len(probabilities)))
        labels = [f"{i:0{n_qubits}b}" for i in indices]
        axis.bar(indices, probabilities, color=["#1c766c" if i == marked else "#b5c6d2" for i in indices])
        ticks = indices if n_qubits <= 4 else sorted({0, marked, len(probabilities) - 1})
        axis.set_xticks(ticks, [labels[i] for i in ticks])
        axis.set(xlabel="Bitstring (most significant bit first)", ylabel="Ideal measurement probability", ylim=(0, 1))
        figure.tight_layout()
        display(figure)
        plt.close(figure)

    live_output = widgets.interactive_output(render_live_case, {
        "n_qubits": n_control, "marked": marked_control, "iterations": iterations_control
    })
    display(widgets.VBox([widgets.HBox([n_control, marked_control, iterations_control]), live_output]))

The MaxCut graph is the cycle with vertices 0,1,2,3 and edges (0,1),(1,2),(2,3),(0,3). The objective is the number of cut edges,C(z)=\sum_{(u,v)}\frac{1-Z_uZ_v}{2}.

Qiskit wire q[0] is the least significant bit. Displayed bitstrings read q[3] q[2] q[1] q[0]. We enumerate all 16 assignments before using a quantum circuit.

For VQE the input is the explicit HamiltonianH=-Z_0-Z_1+\tfrac12X_0X_1.

The independent NumPy matrix uses basis order |00\rangle,|01\rangle,|10\rangle,|11\rangle. Exact diagonalization is a reference calculation on this four-dimensional input.

edges = tuple(opt.CYCLE_EDGES)
n_qubits = 4
cut_values = np.array([
    sum(((assignment >> u) & 1) != ((assignment >> v) & 1) for u, v in edges)
    for assignment in range(2**n_qubits)
], dtype=float)
np.testing.assert_array_equal(opt.maxcut_values(n_qubits, edges), cut_values)
classical_cut_optimum = float(cut_values.max())
classical_best_strings = [f"{i:04b}" for i in np.flatnonzero(cut_values == classical_cut_optimum)]

I = np.eye(2)
X = np.array([[0., 1.], [1., 0.]])
Z = np.diag([1., -1.])
independent_hamiltonian = -np.kron(I, Z) - np.kron(Z, I) + .5*np.kron(X, X)
np.testing.assert_allclose(opt.vqe_hamiltonian(), independent_hamiltonian, atol=1e-14, rtol=0)
exact_eigenvalues = np.linalg.eigvalsh(independent_hamiltonian)
exact_ground_energy = float(exact_eigenvalues[0])
np.testing.assert_allclose(exact_ground_energy, -np.sqrt(4.25), atol=1e-14, rtol=0)
print({"MaxCut optimum": classical_cut_optimum, "optimal bitstrings": classical_best_strings,
       "Hamiltonian eigenvalues": exact_eigenvalues.tolist()})

records.content:
Depth-one QAOA prepares |+\rangle^{\otimes4}, applies e^{-i\gamma C}, then e^{-i\beta\sum_jX_j}. Each cost edge is implemented by CX; RZ(-gamma); CX; its omitted global phase does not affect the output. The mixer uses RX(2 beta). The minimizer receives -\langle C\rangle.

The VQE circuit prepares R_Y(\theta) on qubit 0 and then CX(0,1). It has state \cos(\theta/2)|00\rangle+\sin(\theta/2)|11\rangle and minimizes \langle H\rangle.

Every objective evaluation below checks the independently derived formulas\langle C\rangle=2+\sin(4\beta)\sin(2\gamma),\qquad
E(\theta)=-2\cos\theta+\tfrac12\sin\theta.

The deterministic coordinate polling optimizer starts with step 0.4 radians, evaluates both directions of each coordinate in a fixed order, accepts an improvement greater than 

10-12, and halves its step when no candidate improves the current value. It stops when the step is below 

10-6 radians or after 128 iterations. Angles are periodic modulo 2\pi. These stopping rules are empirical search settings, not a bound on the objective gap.

All three initializations are fixed below. The first run is selected for plots and sampled readout in advance. The complete canonical traces, including every trial objective and measured optimizer time, are in the downloadable runs.json and evaluations.csv. This notebook executes new reproductions; its measured times can differ from those artifacts.

def checked_qaoa_objective(parameters):
    gamma, beta = parameters
    observed = opt.qaoa_expectation(n_qubits, edges, [gamma], [beta])
    predicted = 2 + np.sin(4*beta)*np.sin(2*gamma)
    np.testing.assert_allclose(observed, predicted, atol=2e-12, rtol=0)
    return -observed


def checked_vqe_objective(parameters):
    theta = parameters[0]
    observed = opt.vqe_expectation(theta)
    predicted = -2*np.cos(theta) + .5*np.sin(theta)
    np.testing.assert_allclose(observed, predicted, atol=2e-12, rtol=0)
    return observed


search_settings = dict(initial_step=.4, step_tolerance=1e-6,
                       improvement_tolerance=1e-12, max_iterations=128)
qaoa_initializations = [(0.2, 0.1), (0.6, 0.4), (-0.3, 0.25)]
vqe_initializations = [(0.6,), (-1.1,), (2.2,)]
qaoa_runs, vqe_runs = [], []
reproduction_seconds = {"qaoa": [], "vqe": []}
for name, objective, starts, destination in (
    ("qaoa", checked_qaoa_objective, qaoa_initializations, qaoa_runs),
    ("vqe", checked_vqe_objective, vqe_initializations, vqe_runs),
):
    for initial in starts:
        started = perf_counter()
        result = opt.pattern_search(objective, initial, objective_method="exact_statevector", **search_settings)
        reproduction_seconds[name].append(perf_counter() - started)
        destination.append(result)

vqe_energy = vqe_result["value"]

assert abs(vqe_energy - exact_ground_energy) < 1e-8
print("All objective evaluations passed their independent analytic checks.")



rows = ["| Workflow / fixed start | Final exact objective | Evaluations | Iterations | Stop | Reproduction seconds |",
        "|---|---:|---:|---:|---|---:|"]
for name, starts, runs in (("QAOA expected cut", qaoa_initializations, qaoa_runs),
                          ("VQE energy", vqe_initializations, vqe_runs)):

Optimization above uses zero shots: each objective is evaluated by an ideal statevector. The following held-out sampling experiments evaluate the first optimized parameters with seeds 7, 19 and 41. They do not train a noisy or sampled optimizer.

For QAOA, a single all-Z measurement of all four qubits supplies every edge contribution and a candidate cut. Each seeded experiment uses 2,048 independently simulated shots.

For VQE, measure both qubits in Z to estimate the joint observable -Z_0-Z_1, preserving the covariance of its terms. In a separate group, apply H to both qubits and measure Z to estimate \tfrac12X_0X_1. Each group uses 2,048 shots per seed. Group sample means are added, and their sample variances determine a descriptive estimated standard error. This standard error is not a confidence or device-error guarantee.

Sampling uses the implementation’s NumPy Generator(PCG64) multinomial sampler from the actual circuit probabilities. The QAOA and VQE Z groups use the listed seed; the independent VQE X stream uses that seed plus 1,000,003. The notebook recomputes every sampled mean and group standard error directly from the returned counts. State preparation and the change of measurement basis are present in the generated circuits. Device noise, mitigation, fault-tolerant synthesis and hardware execution time are excluded.

shots_per_group = 2048
sampling_seeds = (7, 19, 41)
z_group_probabilities = Statevector.from_instruction(opt.build_vqe_circuit(theta, basis="z")).probabilities()
x_group_probabilities = Statevector.from_instruction(opt.build_vqe_circuit(theta, basis="x")).probabilities()
indices_two = np.arange(4)
z0 = 1-2*(indices_two & 1)
z1 = 1-2*((indices_two >> 1) & 1)
z_group_values = -z0-z1
x_group_values = .5*z0*z1
np.testing.assert_allclose(np.dot(z_group_probabilities, z_group_values)
                           + np.dot(x_group_probabilities, x_group_values),
                           vqe_energy, atol=1e-12, rtol=0)


def observed_mean_and_standard_error(counts_by_bitstring, values):
    counts = np.array([counts_by_bitstring.get(f"{index:0{int(np.log2(len(values)))}b}", 0)
                       for index in range(len(values))])
    count = int(np.sum(counts))
    mean = float(np.dot(counts, values)/count)
    variance = float(np.dot(counts, (values-mean)**2)/(count-1))
    return mean, np.sqrt(variance/count)


sample_records = []
for seed in sampling_seeds:
    q_readout = opt.sample_qaoa(gamma, beta, shots=shots_per_group, seed=seed)
    v_readout = opt.sample_vqe(theta, shots=shots_per_group, seed=seed)
    q_mean, q_se = observed_mean_and_standard_error(q_readout["counts"], cut_values)
    z_group, x_group = v_readout["groups"]
    z_mean, z_se = observed_mean_and_standard_error(z_group["counts"], z_group_values)
    x_mean, x_se = observed_mean_and_standard_error(x_group["counts"], x_group_values)
    np.testing.assert_allclose([q_mean, q_se],
                               [q_readout["estimate"], q_readout["estimated_standard_error"]],
                               atol=1e-12, rtol=0)
    np.testing.assert_allclose([z_mean+x_mean, np.hypot(z_se, x_se)],
                               [v_readout["estimate"], v_readout["estimated_standard_error"]],
                               atol=1e-12, rtol=0)
    assert sum(q_readout["counts"].values()) == shots_per_group
    assert sum(z_group["counts"].values()) == shots_per_group
    assert sum(x_group["counts"].values()) == shots_per_group
    sample_records.append({"seed": seed, "qaoa": q_readout, "vqe": v_readout})
rows = ["| Seed | Sampled mean cut | Cut SE | Optimal-cut fraction | Sampled VQE energy | Energy SE |",
        "|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|"]
for record in sample_records:
    q, v = record["qaoa"], record["vqe"]
    rows.append(f"| {record['seed']} | {q['estimate']:.6f} | {q['estimated_standard_error']:.6f} | "
                f"{q['optimal_cut_sample_fraction']:.6f} | {v['estimate']:.6f} | {v['estimated_standard_error']:.6f} |")
display_result_table(rows)
print({"exact-optimization shots": 0, "sampled QAOA shots across three seeds": 3*shots_per_group,
       "sampled VQE shots across three seeds and two groups": 3*2*shots_per_group,
       "combined sampled shots": 3*3*shots_per_group})

A complete hybrid run includes the classical input, every accepted and rejected optimizer trial, circuit preparation and evaluation, optimizer control time, and final sampled readout. A statevector objective is a classical numerical calculation and has no measured quantum shot budget. Converting this search into a hardware optimizer would require a new shot allocation and stopping analysis; its cost is not silently inferred from one ansatz circuit.

The generated resource ledger records both the full exact-simulation workload and the separate sampled workload, including measurement groups, repetitions and logical circuit counts. It leaves arbitrary-rotation synthesis and physical resources explicitly pending. The existing Grover surface-code baseline is unchanged.

For the complete canonical artifacts, download runs.json, evaluations.csv, logical-resources.json, the measured qaoa.qasm, vqe-z.qasm, vqe-x.qasm, and the implementation from the optimization chapter. Their reported optimizer times are measurements of that generation run, not portable performance claims. The notebook’s regenerated traces and sample_records remain available in its kernel for inspection.

Grover chapter: initialization, the explicit equality predicate, diffusion, and final measurements. It uses the open-source 

Microsoft Quantum Development Kit and its local qdk.qre estimator. The baseline is a gate-based rotated surface code with round-based magic-state factories.

These results describe an illustrative hardware model. They do not establish an application speedup or a measured hardware performance guarantee. The equality oracle tests a known three-bit string; an application predicate or database access would need its own implementation and cost.

The three algorithm qubits do not translate into three logical compute qubits under the estimator’s scheduling model. Its logical ancillas, data code distance, and factories contribute to the physical count. These overheads can dominate a very small circuit; they are included rather than amortized over an unspecified larger workload.

For this instance, the exported rotations are exact Clifford or T operations. The QDK canonical application trace requires 28 T states and three measurements, with no arbitrary-angle rotation synthesis. The estimator abstracts Clifford work and scheduling into its resource model, so the reported runtime is a model estimate rather than an exact schedule of the original Qiskit circuit. The initial pipeline rejects arbitrary-angle traces until their approximation-error budget is specified.

The two profiles use physical error rates of 

10-3 and 

10-4, 100 ns gate time, and 500 ns measurement time. These are editable model inputs, not benchmarks from a specific processor. The estimator explores the rotated surface-code and round-based factory model combinations and returns a Pareto frontier.

For the default example, one state is marked among eight and two Grover iterations are used. The ideal success probability per circuit execution isp_{\mathrm{success}} = \sin^2\!\left(5\arcsin(1/\sqrt{8})\right) = 0.9453125.

We set an overall failure target of 1%, reserve 0.5% for sampling failure and 0.5% for physical faults, and run two trials serially. Ideal sampling failure is (1-p_{\mathrm{success}})^2\approx0.002991. Each trial receives a physical-failure allowance of 0.25%. A union bound gives overall failure at most 0.7991% under the declared model and ideal verification assumptions. The report records the tighter bound from each returned estimate.

Peak physical qubits remain the per-trial peak because trials run serially. Runtime is multiplied by two. Quantum measurement time is included; classical verification and circuit compilation time are currently unmeasured and excluded. An application with input loading or a more complex predicate must extend this boundary before its estimate can be called end to end.

The estimator consumes the fully decomposed OpenQASM 3 file and records its SHA-256 digest. It rejects missing measurements and remaining custom gate declarations. Changing the qubit count or iteration count requires generating a matching circuit and passing matching --n-qubits, --marked, and --iterations arguments to the estimator. Package versions are embedded in the report.

Add explicit reversible application predicates and state preparation, with loading and classical-output costs.

Use

Compare factory choices, arithmetic, synthesis precision, and scheduling under the same input instance and error target.

Compare later co-designs using matched assumptions and physical qubit/runtime frontiers, retaining this surface-code report as the reference.

The project grows by completing reproducible examples within a stable chapter structure. The survey 

Dalzell et al., 2025 guides coverage; implementation order also reflects which algorithms share reusable circuit and estimation components.

The current release includes Grover, checked Hamiltonian product formulas,
postselected Taylor-LCU and a QSP cosine component, plus QAOA/VQE toy workflows.
It adds independent notebooks, logical workloads, per-algorithm verification,
and physics/math/fault-tolerance appendices. Physical estimates beyond the
frozen Grover baseline remain pending.

The next simulation increment advances complex Hamiltonian evolution,
open-system circuits and thermal preparation. Optimization is adding actual

These stages are implementation milestones. They do not imply that later families are less important or that a quantum advantage is established.

A chapter is complete when it has:

A precise task, access model, input instance, accuracy target, and success criterion.

A small circuit generated from the same implementation used for larger sizes.

A downloadable notebook and a parameterized code entry point with a pinned environment.

A check against a classical result or another independent reference.

Logical-resource accounting that includes the oracle or state preparation.

A physical-resource estimate with its code, hardware assumptions, compilation choices, and error budget.

Paper citations, software attribution, licenses, and a record of the tested version.

An incomplete item remains marked planned, partial, or unavailable. A successful small simulation does not establish scalable performance.

Early work should create components that later chapters can reuse:

Circuit generators with explicit register conventions and ancilla cleanup.

State preparation, controlled operations, and reversible arithmetic.

A common logical-resource record: qubits, operations, depth, precision, and repetitions.

A physical-estimation interface that records the model rather than hiding its assumptions.

A consistent method for saving figures, results, environment versions, and references.

The initial comparison point is a named surface-code model. Later work may change synthesis, arithmetic, scheduling, factory choices, error correction, or the application representation. Each comparison will preserve the task’s input, output, accuracy, and success requirements, then report both the resource change and the extra assumptions.
